To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
geographical distance and the construction of new reactors moderated the effect of the Fukushima accident on public support for nuclear energy.

1) support for nuclear energy decreases more in countries closer to the Fukushima accident and where new nuclear reactors are under construction; 2) freedom of the press does not determine the change in support for the nuclear energy after the accident.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of national factors in opinion change after the 2011 Fukushima nuclear accident and the role of media.
the question of how national context moderates opinion change in the aftermath of a nuclear accident.
the role of the national context in opinion change.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
national context does matter but not as much as previous studies have assumed.

the Fukushima accident did not have a significant impact on public support for nuclear energy in most countries, except for the countries that are closer to Japan or that are building nuclear reactors.

geographical distance from a nuclear accident and the status of new nuclear reactors in a country are the most relevant national contextual variables to consider for the development of nuclear policy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Fukushima accident was a global event and the effects on public opinion are global.
the Fukushima accident had a strong effect on public opinion change, but national context only had limited moderating effect on the change.
geographical distance and the building of a new nuclear power plant were the only national contexts that mattered.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of national context should be tested for each focusing event separately, and that the effect of geographical distance should not be overlooked.
the role of national contextual variables on opinion change following an environmental disaster is more complex than previously thought.
policy makers need to focus on how the accident is framed and communicated, rather than on national context.
